    AI Overview

    AI Mode replied:

    A rainbow is formed when sunlight passes through falling rain or water droplets in the atmosphere, working through three main physical steps: refraction, reflection, and dispersion. 
    How the Process Works
    • Refraction (Bending): White sunlight enters a water droplet from the air. Because water is denser than air, the light slows down and bends (refracts) at the surface. 
    • Dispersion (Separating Colors): White light is actually a mix of many colors, each with a different wavelength. As the light bends, different colors separate at slightly different angles. Violet and blue bend the most, while red and orange bend the least. 
    • Reflection (Bouncing):
      The separated light hits the back side of the raindrop and reflects (bounces) off the inner surface.
       
    • Second Refraction (Exiting): As the light leaves the droplet and re-enters the air, it bends one more time, spreading the colors even further apart. 
    Key Conditions to See a Rainbow
    • Position of the Sun: The sun must be behind you (the observer) and low in the sky, while the rain or mist must be in front of you.
    • Viewing Angle: The light exits the raindrops at an angle of about 42 degrees for a primary rainbow.
    • Full Circle vs. Arc: A rainbow is actually a complete circle, but from the ground, we only see a semi-circle because the horizon blocks the rest. From an airplane, a full circular rainbow can sometimes be visible. 
    You can read more about optical phenomena through the National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service.

    How is a rainbow formed in short answer?
    AI Overview

    AI Mode replied:

    A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through water droplets in the air and undergoes three steps: refraction, reflection, and dispersion. 
    According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the process works like this: 
    • Refraction (Bending): As sunlight enters a raindrop, it slows down and bends because water is denser than air
      .
    • Reflection (Bouncing): The light reflects off the inner back surface of the droplet.
    • Dispersion (Splitting): As the light leaves the droplet, it bends a second time and splits into its component colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet) because different colors travel at different wavelengths. 
    To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain must be in front of you at an angle of about 42 degrees.

      How rare is a 2 rainbow?
      AI Overview

      AI Mode replied:

      Double rainbows are not extremely rare; roughly 1 in every 5 standard rainbows includes a visible secondary arc, meaning there is about a 20% chance of seeing one when rainbow conditions are right. 
      Key Facts About Double Rainbows
      • How They Form: They happen when sunlight reflects twice inside a raindrop instead of once. 
      • Appearance: The second (outer) arc is fainter because light is lost with each reflection, and the color order is reversed (violet on top, red on the bottom). 
      • Best Conditions: You are most likely to spot them early in the morning or late in the afternoon when the sun is low in the sky, with heavy moisture or large raindrops opposite the sun
        .
         
      • Rarer Variations: While standard double rainbows are fairly common, true twinned rainbows (two separate arcs splitting from one base) or higher-order rainbows (third or fourth bows) are genuinely rare.
